chunks.title: Fogged windows, explained
chunks.heading: Fogged windows, explained
chunks.text:
Fogged windows, explained

Why Washington windows fog, how to tell room-side condensation from a failed sealed unit, and when replacement is the only real fix.

Not all “foggy windows” are the same job. One kind is a failed window. The other is your house telling you it is damp.

chunks.title: Fogged windows, explained
chunks.heading: Fog between the panes
chunks.text:
## Fog between the panes

Look at the glass from an angle. If the haze, mineral dots, or film sit *inside* the two panes — where a cloth cannot reach — the insulated glass unit has lost its seal.

That seal is what holds the dry air or argon between the panes. Once it fails:

- The view stays cloudy
- The unit loses most of its insulating value
- The fog can come and go with the weather, then settle in

This is common on older double-pane units after years of sun, movement, and Washington wet-dry cycling.

chunks.title: Fogged windows, explained
chunks.heading: Moisture on the room side
chunks.text:
## Moisture on the room side

If you can wipe the water off the *inside* of the glass, the window may still be doing its job. Warm indoor air hit cold glass and dropped its water there. Showers, cooking, and a house that does not vent well make it worse, especially on single-pane or metal-frame windows.

That is a humidity and glass-temperature problem. Better fans help. A tighter, warmer replacement unit also helps because the indoor face of the glass stays closer to room temperature.

chunks.title: Fogged windows, explained
chunks.heading: What replacement changes
chunks.text:
## What replacement changes

A new insulated unit with a sound spacer and a tight frame does two different things:

- It removes the failed, cloudy glass
- It raises the inside glass temperature so everyday winter condensation is less likely

It will not fix a crawl space that pumps moisture or a bath fan that does not reach outside. We will say so if that is what we see.

chunks.title: Fogged windows, explained
chunks.heading: A simple check before you call
chunks.text:
## A simple check before you call

1. Try to wipe the haze. If it does not move, the unit has failed.
2. Note how many openings look like that.
3. Check the sill for soft wood. Failed glass plus a wet sill is a full-frame conversation.

Bring those notes to an estimate. We will tell you which units are done and which can wait.

chunks.title: Full-frame vs insert replacement
chunks.heading: Full-frame vs insert replacement
chunks.text:
Full-frame vs insert replacement

The difference between insert (pocket) windows and full-frame replacement, and how we choose a method for Washington homes.

There are two honest ways to put a new window in an old opening. The right one depends on the frame that is already there, not on a sales package.

chunks.title: Full-frame vs insert replacement
chunks.heading: Insert, or pocket, replacement
chunks.text:
## Insert, or pocket, replacement

The old sash comes out. The existing frame stays. A new window is built to sit inside that frame.

Choose this when:

- The frame is solid, square, and dry
- Exterior trim and siding are worth keeping
- You want less disruption inside the rooms

Watch-outs: you give up a little glass area, and any rot hiding in that old frame stays hidden. If we see soft wood or a racked opening, we will not force an insert.

chunks.title: Full-frame vs insert replacement
chunks.heading: Full-frame replacement
chunks.text:
## Full-frame replacement

The entire old window comes out to the rough opening. We flash the opening, set a new unit, and close the interior and exterior finishes back up.

Choose this when:

- The frame is rotten, out of square, or aluminum that has had it
- You want to change the look of the exterior casing
- Water has already been in the wall

It is more work. It is also the only way to start over at the opening — which is what a wet Washington wall often needs.

chunks.title: Full-frame vs insert replacement
chunks.heading: How we decide on site
chunks.text:
## How we decide on site

We do not pick a method from a photo of the glass. We look at:

- The sill and stool with a probe, not just an eye
- Whether the sash still closes square
- How the exterior cladding meets the old casing
- Whether you want the same sightlines or a different window style

Then the estimate lists the method per opening, not one price that hides a worse job.

chunks.title: Full-frame vs insert replacement
chunks.heading: What this means for cost and time
chunks.text:
## What this means for cost and time

Inserts are usually faster and cost less per opening. Full-frame takes more crew time and more finish work. A mixed house is normal. Read [what a Washington project costs](/guides/window-replacement-cost-washington) for ranges, then get a measure so the number is about *your* openings.

chunks.title: Signs you need new windows
chunks.heading: Signs you need new windows
chunks.text:
Signs you need new windows

Six practical signs a Washington home is ready for window replacement — drafts, fogged glass, sticky sashes, soft sills, and uneven rooms.

Windows rarely fail all at once. They leak a little more air, collect a little more water, and get a little harder to live with. These are the signs that replacement is the honest next step.

chunks.title: Signs you need new windows
chunks.heading: 1. You can feel weather next to a closed window
chunks.text:
## 1. You can feel weather next to a closed window

A working window should not throw a draft onto the sofa. If you feel air at the lock, the meeting rail, or the stool, the weatherstrip or the frame has given up. In a long Washington heating season that is money and comfort leaving the same opening every day.

chunks.title: Signs you need new windows
chunks.heading: 2. There is fog or haze between the panes
chunks.text:
## 2. There is fog or haze between the panes

That cloud sits inside the insulated glass. You cannot wipe it off. The seal failed, the gas is gone, and the unit no longer insulates the way it was built to. See [fogged windows](/guides/fogged-windows).

chunks.title: Signs you need new windows
chunks.heading: 3. Sashes stick, will not stay open, or will not lock
chunks.text:
## 3. Sashes stick, will not stay open, or will not lock

Paint, swelling, and a frame that is no longer square all show up as hardware that fights you. A tune-up is worth trying once. If the opening itself has moved, a new unit — often a [full-frame replacement](/guides/full-frame-vs-insert) — is cleaner than another round of planing.

chunks.title: Signs you need new windows
chunks.heading: 4. The sill is soft, stained, or peeling
chunks.text:
## 4. The sill is soft, stained, or peeling

Western Washington rain finds the weak corner of a window. Soft wood at the sill or stool means water has been in the opening. Replacement is the chance to flash the opening correctly, not just drop new glass into a wet hole.

chunks.title: Signs you need new windows
chunks.heading: 5. One room never matches the rest of the house
chunks.text:
## 5. One room never matches the rest of the house

Old single-pane and tired aluminum frames create cold glass. The furnace runs, the thermostat is happy, and the chair by the window is not. That is a comfort problem first. Energy savings come along with it.

chunks.title: Signs you need new windows
chunks.heading: 6. The bill went up and nothing else changed
chunks.text:
## 6. The bill went up and nothing else changed

Windows are a small part of the wall and a large part of heat loss. If insulation and the heating system are already decent, leaky glass is a common leftover. Replacement will not make a leaky attic disappear — but it will stop the openings you can feel.

chunks.title: Signs you need new windows
chunks.heading: What to do with this list
chunks.text:
## What to do with this list

If two or more of these are true in the same room, a measure is worth the time. Bring a photo of the elevation and a rough count. We will tell you whether the frames can stay ([insert](/guides/full-frame-vs-insert)) or whether the opening needs to be rebuilt.

chunks.title: Window replacement cost in Washington
chunks.heading: Window replacement cost in Washington
chunks.text:
Window replacement cost in Washington

What drives the price of replacement windows in Washington — method, material, glass, and access — plus honest ranges and what a measure is for.

A window price on the internet is a guess about someone else’s house. The number that matters is the one that follows a measure. This page is here so that number is not a surprise.

chunks.title: Window replacement cost in Washington
chunks.heading: What you are actually paying for
chunks.text:
## What you are actually paying for

Four things move the bid:

1. **Method.** [Insert vs full-frame](/guides/full-frame-vs-insert) changes labor and finish work more than most product upgrades.
2. **Material and line.** Vinyl is the Washington workhorse. Fiberglass costs more and can be the right call on larger or darker-colored units. Within either, a step up in the window line itself — Cascade to Milgard — adds cost per opening for the same install labour.
3. **Glass.** Double-pane low-E is the baseline. Triple-pane, specialty sizes, and tempered glass add cost because they add performance or code.
4. **Access.** A first-floor slider is not a third-story picture window over a roof.

Permits, if the city requires them for the scope, sit on top of that.

chunks.title: Window replacement cost in Washington
chunks.heading: Ranges, not quotes
chunks.text:
## Ranges, not quotes

Industry write-ups for Washington in 2026 often land around **$600 to $1,300 per typical opening** for standard energy-efficient vinyl, with Seattle-area labor on the higher end of that band. A small handful of windows can land in the low thousands. A mid-size house is often a five-figure project.

Treat those as orientation. Your openings, your trim, and your method will move the number.

chunks.title: Window replacement cost in Washington
chunks.heading: How to think about value
chunks.text:
## How to think about value

Replacement is not a utility-bill gadget. The usual reasons it pays are mixed:

- Rooms you can sit in during January
- Glass you can see through
- A dry sill instead of a slow leak
- Less work for the heating system on a long gray season

If someone promises a two-year payback from energy alone, ask them to show the math for *your* existing glass. Single-pane to a modern unit is a different story than already-decent double-pane.

chunks.title: Window replacement cost in Washington
chunks.heading: Rebates in 2026
chunks.text:
## Rebates in 2026

The federal 25C window credit is over for new 2026 installs. Some utilities in Washington still rebate qualifying U-factors, especially when you are replacing single-pane or very poor metal-frame units. Programs differ by city and fuel. We will not print a rebate on an estimate unless it still exists for your meter.

chunks.title: Window replacement cost in Washington
chunks.heading: What an estimate from us includes
chunks.text:
## What an estimate from us includes

- Method per opening
- Product and glass
- Labor, haul-away, and basic finish
- Lead time
- Anything we will *not* do (hidden rot, paint, etc.)

You do not need a perfect window count to start. A few elevation photos and a walkthrough get us there.
